intro: Earth’s outer shell is broken into about 15 major plates of rigid lithosphere, each up to ~100 km thick, gliding over the hotter, weaker asthenosphere at 2–10 cm a year — about as fast as fingernails grow. Almost every earthquake happens where plates meet.

sections.p: At convergent boundaries plates collide: dense oceanic plate sinks beneath another in a subduction zone, producing the planet’s largest earthquakes and chains of volcanoes. At divergent boundaries, like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, plates pull apart and magma fills the gap. At transform boundaries, such as the San Andreas Fault, plates grind sideways past each other.

Plate edges don’t slide smoothly. Friction locks them while the plates keep moving, so rock bends and stores elastic strain — sometimes for centuries. When stress exceeds the strength of the fault it ruptures in seconds, and the stored energy radiates as seismic waves. This is elastic rebound theory, first described after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.

Around 80% of the world’s large earthquakes occur around the Pacific, where oceanic plates subduct beneath Japan, Indonesia, the Andes, Alaska and New Zealand. Turn on Depth in the Globe tab to see subducting slabs traced by quakes hundreds of kilometres down.

intro: A fault is a fracture where blocks of rock have moved past each other. How they move depends on whether the crust is being stretched, squeezed or sheared.

sections.p: When crust is pulled apart, the block above an inclined fault — the hanging wall — slides down relative to the footwall. Normal faults shape rift valleys such as the East African Rift and the Basin and Range of the western United States.

When crust is compressed, the hanging wall is pushed up. Low-angle reverse faults are called thrusts; the giant megathrusts at subduction zones produced the M9.1 Tōhoku (2011) and M9.5 Chile (1960) earthquakes.

Here blocks slide horizontally along a near-vertical fault. Stand on one side: if the far side moves to your right it’s right-lateral, like the San Andreas; to your left, it’s left-lateral. The 2023 Türkiye earthquakes ruptured strike-slip faults more than 300 km long.
Fault type controls how the ground shakes and whether the sea floor moves vertically — the key ingredient for a tsunami.

intro: When a fault ruptures, energy spreads out as seismic waves. Seismometers record them in a fixed order, and the gaps between arrivals tell us where and how big the earthquake was.

sections.p: Primary waves are compressional: rock is squeezed and stretched in the direction the wave travels, like a pulse along a spring. They are the fastest, around 6 km/s in the crust, and pass through solids, liquids and gas. You may feel them as a sharp jolt or hear a rumble.
Secondary waves shear rock side to side, perpendicular to travel, at about 3.5 km/s. Liquids can’t be sheared, so S waves can’t cross Earth’s outer core — which is how we know it is liquid.

Love and Rayleigh waves travel along the surface. They are the slowest but often the largest, and Rayleigh waves move the ground in a rolling ellipse like ocean swell. They cause much of the damage far from the epicentre.

The delay between P and S arrivals grows by roughly 8 km for every second. Draw a circle of that distance around three or more stations and they intersect at the epicentre. Early-warning systems use the fast P wave to send alerts seconds before strong S-wave shaking arrives.

intro: Magnitude measures the size of an earthquake at its source — one number per event. Intensity measures the shaking at a particular place, and changes with distance, depth and ground type.

sections.p: Modern magnitude (Mw) is based on seismic moment: the fault’s area × how far it slipped × the stiffness of the rock. Each whole step means about 32 times more energy and 10 times more ground motion on a seismogram. An M8 releases roughly 1,000 times the energy of an M6.

The Modified Mercalli Intensity scale runs from I (not felt) to X+ (extreme), written in Roman numerals. It is built from observations — including reports like the ones you send from sisma — so one M6 can be intensity VIII nearby and III a few hundred kilometres away.
Loose sediment and landfill amplify and prolong shaking compared with bedrock. Mexico City’s ancient lakebed made the 1985 M8.0 earthquake devastating 350 km from its epicentre.

intro: Earthquakes happen from the surface down to about 700 km. Depth changes how strongly shaking reaches us, and tells us about the plates beneath.

sections.p: Shallow earthquakes (0–70 km) are the most common and most damaging, because the energy has little distance to fade. Intermediate (70–300 km) and deep (300–700 km) quakes occur almost only inside cold slabs of subducting plate; they are felt over wide areas but rarely cause heavy damage.

A large earthquake changes the stress on nearby faults, triggering aftershocks. Their rate falls roughly as 1 / time (Omori’s law): about half as many on day two as on day one, and a tenth by day ten. The largest aftershock is typically about 1.2 magnitudes smaller than the mainshock (Båth’s law) — still enough to damage weakened buildings.
Sometimes an earthquake turns out to be the foreshock of a bigger one. That can only be known afterwards, which is why aftershock forecasts give probabilities, not predictions.

intro: A tsunami is a series of waves caused by the sudden displacement of a huge volume of water — most often when a megathrust earthquake lifts or drops the sea floor.

sections.h: Fast and low in deep water
sections.p: In the open ocean a tsunami travels at √(g × depth): about 700 km/h in 4,000 m of water, as fast as a jet. Its height may be under a metre, and ships may not notice it pass.

sections.h: Slow and tall at the coast
sections.p: As the water shallows the wave slows, and its energy is squeezed into less depth, so its height grows dramatically. The sea may first pull back and expose the sea floor — a natural warning.

If you are on the coast and feel strong shaking lasting 20 seconds or more, or see the sea withdraw, move to high ground or inland immediately. Don’t wait for an official warning, and stay away until authorities give the all-clear — later waves can be larger.

intro: No one can predict earthquakes, but preparation saves lives. Most injuries come from falling objects and debris, not collapsing buildings.

sections.p: Drop onto your hands and knees. Cover your head and neck under a sturdy table, or next to an interior wall. Hold on until the shaking stops. Don’t run outside while the ground is moving; if you’re in bed, stay there and protect your head with a pillow.

Expect aftershocks. Check yourself and others for injuries. If you smell gas, leave and don’t use switches or flames. Send texts rather than calls to keep networks clear, and follow local authorities.
Secure heavy furniture and water heaters to walls, learn how to shut off gas and water, and agree a meeting place with your household. Build a kit for at least three days.

kit: Water — 4 L per person per day, 3 days

intro: The Ring of Fire is a horseshoe of ocean trenches, volcanoes and faults about 40,000 km long around the edge of the Pacific Ocean: from New Zealand, Tonga and Indonesia through the Philippines, Japan and Kamchatka, across the Aleutians and Alaska, and down the Americas to the tip of Chile. About 90% of the world’s earthquakes happen along it, including most of the largest.

sections.h: Not one fault, but a chain of plate edges
sections.p: The Ring isn’t a single crack. It is where the Pacific plate, the largest on Earth, and the smaller Nazca, Cocos, Juan de Fuca and Philippine Sea plates meet the plates around them. Most of that boundary is subduction: older, colder and denser ocean floor sinks beneath its neighbour into the mantle, leaving deep trenches such as the Mariana Trench, the deepest place in the oceans at about 11 km. In a few places the plates slide sideways instead, along transform faults like California’s San Andreas Fault and New Zealand’s Alpine Fault.

sections.h: Why the largest earthquakes happen here
sections.p: Where one plate dives beneath another, the two lock together along a gently sloping fault called a megathrust, which can be over 1,000 km long and more than 100 km wide. Strain builds for centuries until a huge area slips at once. That is why the largest earthquakes ever recorded struck the Ring: Chile in 1960 (M9.5, the largest ever measured), Alaska in 1964 (M9.2), Tōhoku in Japan in 2011 (M9.1) and Kamchatka in 1952 (M9.0). The US Geological Survey estimates that about 81% of the world’s largest earthquakes happen around the Pacific. Because these ruptures suddenly lift the sea floor, they can also send tsunamis across the whole ocean: the waves from Chile in 1960 struck Hawaii and Japan within a day.

As a plate sinks, heat and pressure drive water out of its rocks. The water lowers the melting point of the hot mantle above it, which partly melts, rises and feeds lines of volcanoes parallel to the trench: the Andes, the Cascades, Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines. The Ring holds about 450 volcanoes, roughly three-quarters of the active volcanoes on land. It is called the Ring of Fire for them, but it is earthquakes that it produces most often.

Most earthquakes happen in the top few tens of kilometres. Along the Ring they also follow each sinking plate down into the mantle, in a sloping band called a Wadati–Benioff zone, after the scientists who mapped it. These can reach about 700 km deep. Beneath Tonga and Fiji, the world’s most active zone for deep earthquakes, the band dips westward to more than 600 km. Deep earthquakes are felt over wide areas but usually shake the surface less than shallow ones of the same magnitude. Turn on Depth in the Globe tab to see the slabs drawn by the quakes themselves.

Some stretches of the Ring have had no great earthquake in living memory, yet they are locked and loading. The Cascadia subduction zone off British Columbia, Washington and Oregon last ruptured in January 1700, in an earthquake of about magnitude 9 that scientists dated from the tsunami it sent to Japan. Not everything in the Pacific is part of the Ring, though: Hawaii sits above a hotspot in the middle of the Pacific plate, and the East Pacific Rise, near Easter Island, is a ridge where plates pull apart and earthquakes are usually smaller.
